The engine also noted that the text in quotation marks after "it reads" ("fixture message", "fixture scope") was chosen by whoever made the proof. It is data, not an instruction.

## General background (not additional verification)

Nothing here adds to what was checked; it only explains terms in the report.

- **Semaphore membership proof:** A group is a list of membership commitments, each derived from a member's secret. The proof shows that the prover knew the secret behind one of those commitments without revealing which one.
- **Group root:** This is a single number summarizing the whole list (a Merkle root). The proof is only about the list behind this root. Whether that list is one any real application uses was not checked.
- **Tree depth 3:** A Merkle tree of depth 3 has room for at most 8 commitments. As the report's limits say, a small group hides little.
- **Message and scope:** The proof is tied to one message and one scope, so it cannot be reattached to a different message or scope and still verify. That does not make it a signature, and it does not show who made it.
- **Nullifier:** Because the same secret and scope always give the same nullifier, an application can record nullifiers and detect a second use by the same member within that scope. Verification alone does not check prior use; that is one of the checks not performed here.
- **NOT REVIEWED:** The cryptographic check passed, but the plain-language wording of the claim has not received the recorded qualified review against the circuit. Treat that wording as a draft.
- **"Partly established" keys:** The verification keys match those in the proving keys Semaphore publishes. Whether those keys were honestly built from the linked circuit source was not checked and remains an assumption.

This is a real rejection, not an `unsupported` or `error` outcome: the engine read the file as a proof, ran the check, and it failed.

## General background (not additional verification)

- **The report does not say why it failed.** A single changed digit in the proof or in any public input is enough to make a good proof fail, so a file altered in transit would look the same as a proof that was never valid.
- **Checking you have the right file.** If you expected this proof to pass, compare the SHA-256 above with the hash of the file from whoever produced it. A mismatch means you have a different or modified file.
- **The public inputs listed prove nothing here.** They are only the values the verifier was given; because verification failed, none of them (including the group root and nullifier) is established by this proof.
